# Part 1: Configure the project and examine the data

## Load packages and prepare the data

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(emmeans)
library(broom.mixed)
library(gt)
library(AER)

# Load the original dataset
data("NMES1988", package = "AER")

# Select the six variables and set reference groups
data <- NMES1988 |>
  dplyr::select(visits, chronic, health, gender, school, insurance) |>
  mutate(
    health = fct_relevel(health, "average"),
    gender = fct_relevel(gender, "male"),
    insurance = fct_relevel(insurance, "no")
  )

# Explicitly set the coding for the reference groups
contrasts(data$health) <- contr.treatment(levels(data$health))
contrasts(data$gender) <- contr.treatment(levels(data$gender))
contrasts(data$insurance) <- contr.treatment(levels(data$insurance))
```

The outcome is the number of physician office visits. Predictors are
the number of chronic conditions, self-perceived health, gender,
years of education, and private insurance coverage.

The reference groups are average health, male, and no insurance.

## Explore the data

```{r}
#| label: outcome-summary

visits_summary <- data |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(visits),
    variance = var(visits),
    proportion_zero = mean(visits == 0),
    maximum = max(visits)
  )

visits_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Descriptive Statistics for Physician Office Visits"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    n = "N",
    mean = "Mean",
    variance = "Variance",
    proportion_zero = "Proportion of zeros",
    maximum = "Maximum"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean, variance, proportion_zero),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt_integer(columns = c(n, maximum))
```

```{r}
#| label: visits-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of physician office visits."

ggplot(data, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of physician office visits",
    y = "Number of respondents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Physician office visits are a count outcome: values are non-negative
whole numbers. Among `r visits_summary$n` respondents, the mean number
of visits was `r round(visits_summary$mean, 2)`, and the variance was
`r round(visits_summary$variance, 2)`. The variance-to-mean ratio was
`r round(visits_summary$variance / visits_summary$mean, 2)`.
Overall, `r round(100 * visits_summary$proportion_zero, 1)`% of
respondents reported no visits, and the maximum was
`r visits_summary$maximum` visits.

# Part 2: Specify competing count models

## Why not a linear model?

```{r}
#| label: gaussian-model

m_gauss <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: gaussian-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the Gaussian model."

set.seed(9041)

res_gauss <- simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = m_gauss,
  n = 500,
  seed = 9041,
  plot = FALSE
)

plot(res_gauss)
```
The Gaussian model showed substantial lack of fit. The DHARMa QQ plot strayed far from the diagonal, and the uniformity and outlier tests were significant. The residual-versus-predicted plot also showed systematic quantile deviations, indicating that the residual distribution varied across fitted values. Even though the dispersion test was not significant, this did not resolve the other diagnostic problems. A Gaussian model also assigns probability to negative and non-integer outcomes, whereas physician visits are non-negative counts, and its constant conditional variance assumption may be unsuitable for this outcome. These findings motivate evaluating count-regression models.

## Specify three nested Poisson models

```{r}
#| label: poisson-models

# M0: Intercept-only model
m0_pois <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ 1,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

# M1: Number of chronic conditions
m1_pois <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)

# M2: Full model
m2_pois <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = poisson(link = "log")
)
```

## Compare the Poisson models

```{r}
#| label: poisson-comparisons

pois_comparison <- anova(m0_pois, m1_pois, m2_pois)

pois_comparison |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Nested Poisson Models"
  )
```
# Part 3: Evaluate the Poisson model

## Simulate residuals

```{r}
#| label: poisson-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the full Poisson model."

set.seed(9041)

res_pois <- simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = m2_pois,
  n = 500,
  seed = 9041,
  plot = FALSE
)

plot(res_pois)
```

## Test for dispersion and excess zeros

```{r}
#| label: poisson-diagnostic-tests

disp_pois <- testDispersion(res_pois)
zi_pois <- testZeroInflation(res_pois)

disp_pois
zi_pois
```
## Interpret the Poisson diagnostics

The full Poisson model showed significant overdispersion
(DHARMa dispersion ratio =
`r round(unname(disp_pois$statistic), 2)`, *p* < .001).
The observed number of zeros was
`r round(unname(zi_pois$statistic), 2)` times the number
expected under the fitted model (*p* < .001).
These results indicate that the Poisson model does not adequately
capture the variability and zeros in the outcome. Overdispersion
can lead to underestimated standard errors, overly narrow
confidence intervals, and overly small p-values. However,
excess zeros relative to the Poisson model do not necessarily
imply a separate zero-generating process. A negative binomial
model will therefore be evaluated before considering a
zero-inflated or hurdle model.

# Part 4: Fit and evaluate a negative binomial model

## Estimate the NB2 model

```{r}
#| label: nb2-model

m_nb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)
```

## Compare the Poisson and NB2 models

```{r}
#| label: poisson-nb2-comparison

lrt_nb <- anova(m2_pois, m_nb)

lrt_nb |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Full Poisson and Negative Binomial Models"
  )
```

## Re-check the NB2 model with DHARMa

```{r}
#| label: nb2-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the NB2 model."

set.seed(9041)

res_nb <- simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = m_nb,
  n = 500,
  seed = 9041,
  plot = FALSE
)

plot(res_nb)
```

```{r}
#| label: nb2-diagnostic-tests

disp_nb <- testDispersion(res_nb)
zi_nb <- testZeroInflation(res_nb)

disp_nb
zi_nb
```
The NB2 model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model,
χ²(`r lrt_nb[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r round(lrt_nb[2, "Chisq"], 2)`, *p* < .001.
The comparison has one degree of freedom because NB2 estimates
an additional dispersion parameter. The NB2 dispersion test
was not significant (ratio =
`r round(unname(disp_nb$statistic), 2)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", disp_nb$p.value)`), indicating that
the previously detected overdispersion was no longer clear
on this diagnostic. So, the Poisson model's restrictive
variance assumption was not supported, and its conventional
standard errors and significance tests should not be relied on
for inference.

However, the NB2 model continued to under predict zeros
(observed/expected ratio =
`r round(unname(zi_nb$statistic), 2)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", zi_nb$p.value)`).
Although this mismatch was much smaller than under Poisson,
the observed number of zeros remained approximately
`r round(100 * (unname(zi_nb$statistic) - 1), 2)`%
greater than expected. So, Zero-inflated and hurdle negative
binomial models will be evaluated.

## Visualize predicted counts

```{r}
#| label: nb2-predicted-counts
#| fig-cap: "Predicted physician visits by number of chronic conditions under NB2."

pred_nb <- predict_response(
  m_nb,
  terms = "chronic [all]"
)

plot(pred_nb) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Physician Visits by Chronic Conditions",
    x = "Number of chronic conditions",
    y = "Predicted physician office visits"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The predicted relationship curves because the NB2 model uses a log link, which makes the predicted relationship curved on the count scale. A one-unit increase in chronic conditions adds a constant amount to the log expected count, corresponding to a multiplicative
change in the expected number of visits.

# Part 5: Decide whether the zeros need their own model

## Decide whether to investigate a separate process for zeros

The NB2 model heavily improved on the Poisson model, but
it still under predicted the number of zeros. Its observed-to-expected
zero ratio was `r round(unname(zi_nb$statistic), 2)`,
with *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", zi_nb$p.value)`.
So, zero-inflated and hurdle negative binomial models
were fitted for comparison with NB2.

## Fit the zero-inflated negative binomial model

```{r}
#| label: zinb-model

m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = nbinom2(link = "log")
)
```

## Fit the hurdle negative binomial model

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-model

m_hurdle <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = truncated_nbinom2(link = "log")
)
```

## Compare NB2 with the zero-inflated model

```{r}
#| label: nb2-zinb-comparison

lrt_zinb <- anova(m_nb, m_zinb)

lrt_zinb
```

## Compare all three models using AIC and BIC

```{r}
#| label: zero-model-information-criteria

zero_aic <- AIC(m_nb, m_zinb, m_hurdle)
zero_bic <- BIC(m_nb, m_zinb, m_hurdle)

zero_aic |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "AIC Comparison of Models")

zero_bic |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "BIC Comparison of Models")
```
## Evaluate the model comparisons

The zero-inflated negative binomial model improved fit relative
to NB2 in the likelihood-ratio comparison,
χ²(`r lrt_zinb[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r round(lrt_zinb[2, "Chisq"], 2)`, *p* < .001.
This test involves a boundary case, so it was considered
alongside the information criteria and residual diagnostics.

Both the zero-inflated and hurdle models had lower AIC and BIC
than ordinary NB2. The hurdle model had the lowest AIC
(`r round(zero_aic["m_hurdle", "AIC"], 2)`) and BIC
(`r round(zero_bic["m_hurdle", "BIC"], 2)`).
Therefore, it was selected for further diagnostic
evaluation.

## Re-check the hurdle model with DHARMa

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the hurdle negative binomial model."

set.seed(9041)

res_hurdle <- simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = m_hurdle,
  n = 500,
  seed = 9041,
  plot = FALSE
)

plot(res_hurdle)
```

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-diagnostic-reporting
#| include: false

disp_hurdle_report <- DHARMa::testDispersion(
  res_hurdle,
  plot = FALSE
)

uniform_hurdle_report <- DHARMa::testUniformity(
  res_hurdle,
  plot = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-diagnostic-tests

disp_hurdle <- testDispersion(res_hurdle)
zi_hurdle <- testZeroInflation(res_hurdle)

disp_hurdle
zi_hurdle
```
The hurdle negative binomial model reproduced the overall number
of zeros well (observed/expected ratio =
`r round(unname(zi_hurdle$statistic), 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", zi_hurdle$p.value)`).
But, the dispersion test remained significant
(ratio = `r round(unname(disp_hurdle$statistic), 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", disp_hurdle$p.value)`),
indicating residual overdispersion. So, although the hurdle
model had the lowest AIC and BIC among the candidates, its
diagnostics did not indicate a fully adequate fit. I also examined the ZINB
model before making the final model choice.

## Examine ZINB diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: zinb-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residual diagnostics for the ZINB model."

set.seed(9041)

res_zinb <- simulateResiduals(
  fittedModel = m_zinb,
  n = 500,
  seed = 9041,
  plot = FALSE
)

plot(res_zinb)
```

```{r}
#| label: zinb-diagnostic-tests

disp_zinb <- testDispersion(res_zinb)
zi_zinb <- testZeroInflation(res_zinb)

disp_zinb
zi_zinb
```
## Justify my choice for which model was carried forward

The hurdle negative binomial model was carried forward because
it had the lowest AIC and BIC of the candidate models and
reproduced the overall number of zeros well
(observed/expected ratio =
`r round(unname(zi_hurdle$statistic), 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", zi_hurdle$p.value)`).
In contrast, ordinary NB2 continued to under predict zeros.
The ZINB model also addressed the overall zero-count mismatch,
but had higher AIC and BIC than the hurdle model.

The selected model nevertheless retained significant residual
overdispersion (ratio =
`r round(unname(disp_hurdle$statistic), 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", disp_hurdle$p.value)`) and its residuals differed significantly from the expected uniform distribution. The quantile
diagnostic also issued a fitting warning, so its p-value was
not relied upon. So, the hurdle model was the best-supported
of the candidates considered, rather than a fully adequate
description of the data. Later findings are interpreted
with this limitation in mind.

# Part 6: Test and probe an interaction

## 6.1 State the prediction

I predict that the positive association between chronic conditions
and physician visits will be stronger for people with private
insurance than among those without it. Private insurance could
reduce financial barriers to seeking care which would allow increases in
healthcare needs to translate into greater use of physician services.
This prediction concerns the interaction in the model's count
component. The zero component is kept unchanged.

## 6.2 Fit the interaction model

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-interaction-model

m_hurdle_int <- glmmTMB(
  visits ~ chronic * insurance + health + gender + school,
  ziformula = ~ chronic + health + gender + school + insurance,
  data = data,
  family = truncated_nbinom2(link = "log")
)
```

## 6.3 Test whether the interaction is needed

The additive and interaction models were compared using a
likelihood-ratio test. The zero component was identical in both
models, so this comparison tests the addition of the
chronic conditions × insurance interaction in the count component.

```{r}
#| label: hurdle-interaction-comparison

lrt_int <- anova(m_hurdle, m_hurdle_int)

lrt_int |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Likelihood-Ratio Test of the Interaction"
  )
```

The likelihood-ratio comparison gave
χ²(`r lrt_int[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r round(lrt_int[2, "Chisq"], 2)`,
`r if (lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"] < .001) "*p* < .001" else paste0("*p* = ", sprintf("%.3f", lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"]))`.

The interaction will be probed regardless of the significance
of this test. Probing examines the association with chronic
conditions within each insurance group and the differences
between insurance groups at selected values of chronic conditions.

Adding the chronic conditions × insurance interaction did not
significantly improve model fit. The estimated interaction was
negative, which was the opposite of the predicted direction, but there was
insufficient evidence that the count-component association
between chronic conditions and physician visits differed by
insurance status. AIC and BIC also favored the simpler additive
model. The interaction model was still retained for
probing, since this assignment requires this. This does not imply
that it was preferred as the final model.

## 6.4 Plot predicted counts

```{r}
#| label: interaction-predicted-counts
#| fig-cap: "Predicted physician visits by chronic conditions and private insurance, incorporating both hurdle-model components."

set.seed(9041)

pred_int <- predict_response(
  m_hurdle_int,
  terms = c("chronic [all]", "insurance"),
  type = "zero_inflated"
)

plot(pred_int) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("no" = "steelblue", "yes" = "darkorange"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("no" = "steelblue", "yes" = "darkorange"),
    labels = c("No", "Yes")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Physician Visits by Chronic Conditions",
    subtitle = "Predictions by private insurance coverage",
    x = "Number of chronic conditions",
    y = "Predicted physician office visits",
    colour = "Private insurance",
    fill = "Private insurance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The plot shows predicted physician visits across chronic conditions
for respondents with and without private insurance. Predictions
incorporate both the probability of having any visits and the
expected positive visit count. Other predictors are held at their
reference categories or means.

## 6.5 Probe the interaction

### Simple slopes of chronic conditions within insurance groups

```{r}
#| label: interaction-simple-slopes

slopes <- emtrends(
  m_hurdle_int,
  specs = ~ insurance,
  var = "chronic",
  component = "cond"
)

slopes_summary <- summary(
  slopes,
  infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)
)

slopes_summary
```

### Compare the two slopes

```{r}
#| label: interaction-slope-comparison

slope_comparison <- pairs(slopes)

summary(
  slope_comparison,
  infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)
)
```

The simple slopes describe the chronic-condition association
within each insurance group on the count-component log scale.
The slope comparison tests whether those two slopes differ.
It does not test the interaction in the model's zero component,
which was kept unchanged.

The count-component slope for chronic conditions was positive
in both insurance groups. But, the difference between the
slopes was not statistically significant, consistent with the
likelihood-ratio test of the interaction. The positive sign of
the slope comparison contrasts with the negative interaction
coefficient because the comparison subtracts the insured slope
from the "without private insurance" slope, whereas the model coefficient uses
the opposite direction. So, the estimates have opposite
signs but the same standard error and two-sided p-value.

### Simple effects of insurance at selected chronic-condition values

```{r}
#| label: interaction-simple-effects

# Calculate the three probing values
chronic_mean <- mean(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)
chronic_sd <- sd(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)

chronic_values <- chronic_mean + c(-1, 0, 1) * chronic_sd

# Estimate insurance-group means on the count-component log scale
insurance_emmeans <- emmeans(
  m_hurdle_int,
  specs = ~ insurance | chronic,
  at = list(chronic = chronic_values),
  component = "cond"
)

# Compare no insurance with insurance at each probing value
simple_effects <- pairs(insurance_emmeans)

simple_effects_summary <- summary(
  simple_effects,
  infer = c(TRUE, TRUE),
  type = "link"
)

simple_effects_summary
```

## 6.6 Report the simple effects in a table

```{r}
#| label: simple-effects-table

simple_effects_df <- as.data.frame(simple_effects_summary) |>
  mutate(
    chronic_level = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")[
      match(chronic, chronic_values)
    ]
  )

simple_effects_df |>
  dplyr::select(
    chronic_level, chronic, contrast,
    estimate, SE, z.ratio, p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Simple Effects of Private Insurance",
    subtitle = "Hurdle negative binomial count component"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    chronic_level = "Probing level",
    chronic = "Chronic conditions",
    contrast = "Contrast",
    estimate = "Log contrast",
    SE = "SE",
    z.ratio = "z",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(chronic, estimate, SE, z.ratio),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
    }
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    "Contrasts are No - Yes. Tests are computed on the count-component log scale. Each probing value is treated as a separate comparison family."
  )
```

### Comparing emmeans results with the prediction plot

The emmeans analyses averaged over health and gender, whereas
the ggeffects plot held non-focal categorical predictors at their
reference levels. For comparisons on the same count-component
log scale, these additive control-variable contributions cancel
from the insurance contrast because they do not interact with
insurance. However, the plotted predictions also combined the
zero and count components, while the simple-effects analysis
used only the count component. So, differences between the
plot and these results reflect both the treatment of control
variables and the model quantity being estimated. The
count-component log contrasts should not be interpreted as
contrasts in overall expected visits.

## 6.7 Interpret the interaction

There was insufficient evidence that the count-component
association between chronic conditions and physician visits
differed by private insurance status. Adding the interaction
did not significantly improve fit,
χ²(`r lrt_int[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r round(lrt_int[2, "Chisq"], 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", lrt_int[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"])`.
The chronic-condition slopes were positive in both insurance
groups, but their difference was not statistically significant.

Simple-effects comparisons indicated that respondents
without private insurance had a lower count-component log
parameter than those with insurance at low chronic conditions
(log contrast =
`r round(simple_effects_df$estimate[1], 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_df$p.value[1])`),
average chronic conditions
(log contrast =
`r round(simple_effects_df$estimate[2], 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_df$p.value[2])`),
and high chronic conditions
(log contrast =
`r round(simple_effects_df$estimate[3], 3)`,
*p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_df$p.value[3])`).
These tests were not adjusted across the three probing values.
The estimated log-scale difference was largest at the low
probing value and smallest at the high value, but the
non-significant interaction does not support a reliable change
in the group difference as chronic conditions increase.

Overall, the results suggest an insurance-group difference in
the count component instead of clear evidence of moderation.
The original prediction of a stronger chronic-condition slope
among respondents with private insurance was not supported. Still, interpretation
remains cautious because the selected model retained
residual-fit limitations.

# Part 7: Results and discussion

```{r}
#| label: results-preparation
#| include: false

# Extract coefficients and 95% Wald confidence intervals
final_coefficients <- broom.mixed::tidy(
  m_hurdle,
  effects = "fixed",
  component = c("cond", "zi"),
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

# Separate the count and zero components
count_results <- final_coefficients |>
  filter(component == "cond")

zero_results <- final_coefficients |>
  filter(component == "zi")
```

## 7.1 Results

```{r}
#| label: model-selection-reporting
#| include: false

pois_nb_comparison <- anova(m2_pois, m_nb)

selection_bic <- BIC(m_nb, m_zinb, m_hurdle)

report_p <- function(p) {
  if (p < .001) {
    "p < .001"
  } else {
    paste0("p = ", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
  }
}
```

Physician visits had a mean of
`r sprintf("%.2f", visits_summary$mean)` and a variance of
`r sprintf("%.2f", visits_summary$variance)`, with
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * visits_summary$proportion_zero)`%
of respondents reporting no visits. The full Poisson model
showed pronounced overdispersion
(dispersion ratio =
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(disp_pois$statistic))`,
`r report_p(disp_pois$p.value)`)
and under predicted the number of zeros
(observed-to-simulated zero ratio =
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(zi_pois$statistic))`,
`r report_p(zi_pois$p.value)`).
The negative-binomial model fit significantly better than
the Poisson model,
χ²(`r pois_nb_comparison[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r sprintf("%.2f", pois_nb_comparison[2, "Chisq"])`,
`r report_p(pois_nb_comparison[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"])`.
The NB2 dispersion test was no longer significant
(dispersion ratio =
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(disp_nb$statistic))`,
`r report_p(disp_nb$p.value)`),
but the model still under predicted zeros
(observed-to-simulated zero ratio =
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(zi_nb$statistic))`,
`r report_p(zi_nb$p.value)`),
supporting consideration of a separate zero component.
Among the NB2, zero-inflated negative-binomial, and hurdle
negative-binomial candidates, the hurdle model had the lowest BIC
(`r sprintf("%.2f", selection_bic["m_hurdle", "BIC"])`),
compared with
`r sprintf("%.2f", selection_bic["m_zinb", "BIC"])`
for the zero-inflated model and
`r sprintf("%.2f", selection_bic["m_nb", "BIC"])`
for NB2, and was carried forward. Still, its residual
diagnostics indicated remaining overdispersion
(dispersion ratio =
`r sprintf("%.3f", unname(disp_hurdle_report$statistic))`,
`r report_p(disp_hurdle_report$p.value)`)
and residuals that differed significantly from the expected
uniform distribution
(D = `r sprintf("%.3f", unname(uniform_hurdle_report$statistic))`,
`r report_p(uniform_hurdle_report$p.value)`).
So, The hurdle model was the best-supported candidate
among those considered, instead of it being a fully adequate model.

```{r}
#| label: format-main-results
#| include: false

format_effect <- function(results, predictor) {
  row <- results[results$term == predictor, ]

  p_text <- if (row$p.value < .001) {
    "p < .001"
  } else {
    paste0("p = ", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", row$p.value)))
  }

  sprintf(
    "b = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], %s",
    row$estimate,
    row$conf.low,
    row$conf.high,
    p_text
  )
}
```

In the selected additive hurdle negative-binomial model, greater
numbers of chronic conditions
(`r format_effect(count_results, "chronic")`),
poor health relative to the reference health category
(`r format_effect(count_results, "healthpoor")`),
more years of schooling
(`r format_effect(count_results, "school")`),
and private insurance
(`r format_effect(count_results, "insuranceyes")`)
were associated with higher log-scale count-component parameters,
while adjusting for the other predictors. Excellent health was associated
with a lower count-component parameter
(`r format_effect(count_results, "healthexcellent")`),
whereas the female–male difference was not statistically significant
(`r format_effect(count_results, "genderfemale")`).
In the zero component, more chronic conditions
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "chronic")`),
female gender
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "genderfemale")`),
more schooling
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "school")`),
and private insurance
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "insuranceyes")`)
were associated with lower odds of reporting zero physician visits.
Excellent health was associated with higher odds of zero visits
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "healthexcellent")`),
whereas poor health was not significantly associated with the odds
of zero visits
(`r format_effect(zero_results, "healthpoor")`).
Count-component coefficients describe the log-scale parameter of
the truncated negative-binomial distribution, instead of effects
on overall expected physician visits.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-reporting
#| include: false

interaction_lrt <- anova(m_hurdle, m_hurdle_int)

interaction_slopes <- as.data.frame(
  emmeans::emtrends(
    m_hurdle_int,
    specs = ~ insurance,
    var = "chronic",
    component = "cond"
  )
)

slope_no <- interaction_slopes[
  as.character(interaction_slopes$insurance) == "no", ]

slope_yes <- interaction_slopes[
  as.character(interaction_slopes$insurance) == "yes", ]
```

```{r}
#| label: interaction-probe-reporting
#| include: false

# Simple slopes, including tests against zero
slopes_report <- as.data.frame(
  summary(
    emmeans::emtrends(
      m_hurdle_int,
      specs = ~ insurance,
      var = "chronic",
      component = "cond"
    ),
    infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)
  )
)

slope_no <- slopes_report[
  as.character(slopes_report$insurance) == "no", ]

slope_yes <- slopes_report[
  as.character(slopes_report$insurance) == "yes", ]

# Insurance comparisons at mean - SD, mean, and mean + SD
chronic_probe_values <- mean(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE) +
  c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(data$chronic, na.rm = TRUE)

insurance_probe <- emmeans::emmeans(
  m_hurdle_int,
  specs = ~ insurance | chronic,
  at = list(chronic = chronic_probe_values),
  component = "cond"
)

simple_effects_report <- as.data.frame(
  summary(
    pairs(insurance_probe, reverse = FALSE, adjust = "none"),
    infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)
  )
)

simple_effects_report <- simple_effects_report[
  order(simple_effects_report$chronic), ]
```

Adding the chronic conditions × private insurance interaction
to the count component did not significantly improve model fit,
χ²(`r interaction_lrt[2, "Chi Df"]`) =
`r sprintf("%.3f", interaction_lrt[2, "Chisq"])`,
`r report_p(interaction_lrt[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"])`.
The count-component log-scale slope for chronic conditions was
positive for respondents without private insurance
(b = `r sprintf("%.3f", slope_no$chronic.trend)`,
95% CI [`r sprintf("%.3f", slope_no$asymp.LCL)`,
`r sprintf("%.3f", slope_no$asymp.UCL)`],
`r report_p(slope_no$p.value)`)
and for those with private insurance
(b = `r sprintf("%.3f", slope_yes$chronic.trend)`,
95% CI [`r sprintf("%.3f", slope_yes$asymp.LCL)`,
`r sprintf("%.3f", slope_yes$asymp.UCL)`],
`r report_p(slope_yes$p.value)`).
Pointwise comparisons indicated lower count-component log
parameters for "without private insurance" than respondents with private insurance at low chronic conditions
(no − yes log contrast =
`r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_report$estimate[1])`,
`r report_p(simple_effects_report$p.value[1])`), average chronic conditions
(log contrast =
`r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_report$estimate[2])`,
`r report_p(simple_effects_report$p.value[2])`),
and high chronic conditions
(log contrast =
`r sprintf("%.3f", simple_effects_report$estimate[3])`,
`r report_p(simple_effects_report$p.value[3])`).
These comparisons were not adjusted across the three probing
values. The estimated log-scale insurance difference was largest
at the low probing value and smallest at the high probing value,
but remained statistically significant at all three values.
However, the non-significant interaction did not support a
reliable difference between the chronic-condition slopes.
The prediction of a stronger positive association among insured
respondents was therefore not supported. So, the additive hurdle
model was retained.

## 7.2 Discussion

The findings suggest that chronic conditions and self-perceived
health were important correlates of physician visits. More chronic
conditions were associated with a higher count-component parameter
and lower odds of reporting no visits, suggesting associations
with both whether respondents visited a physician and the
positive-count process. Compared with average health, poor health
was associated with a higher count-component parameter, whereas
excellent health was associated with a lower count-component
parameter and higher odds of reporting no visits. Together, these
patterns are consistent with greater healthcare use among
respondents with greater health needs. However, coefficient
magnitudes should not be used alone to rank the importance of
predictors because the predictors have different measurement
scales.

Private insurance and education were also associated with both
components of physician use. Respondents with private insurance and those with
more schooling had higher count-component parameters and lower
odds of zero visits, holding the other predictors constant.
Women had lower odds of zero visits than men, but the
count-component gender difference was not statistically
significant. There was insufficient evidence that private
insurance moderated the association between chronic conditions
and the count component. Although insurance-group differences
were detected at each selected chronic-condition value, those
differences did not establish that the chronic-condition slopes
differed between groups.

Many limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. 
The analysis was observational, so the associations do not establish causal
effects. The selected model adjusted only for the included
predictors. Other factors, such as income and access to care,
could contribute to the observed associations. The data concern
older adults surveyed in the United States in the late 1980s,
which limits generalization to younger populations and
contemporary healthcare settings. Most importantly, although
the hurdle negative-binomial model was the best-supported
candidate among those considered, its residual diagnostics
still indicated overdispersion and residuals that differed
significantly from the expected uniform distribution. So, we should interpret its standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values cautiously. The simple-effects tests
were also pointwise comparisons without adjustment across
the three probing values. Finally, count-component coefficients
describe the truncated distribution's log-scale parameter,
not overall expected visits, which depend on both hurdle
components.
